title: SciLENS: RL-Driven Autonomous Agents for Scientific Localized Evidence Navigation and Synthesis
abstract: Scientific literature synthesis agents increasingly rely on proprietary online services, limiting reproducibility, privacy, and offline deployment. To address this challenge, we introduce SciLENS Scientific Localized Evidence Navigation and Synthesis), a fully local autonomous agent framework operating on a dual-tier infrastructure indexing approximately 12 million academic records. SciLENS pioneers the integration of structural visualization as an actionable tool within the reasoning loop, enabling the agent to compress complex citation topologies into validated data-driven charts and thereby mitigate context exhaustion during macro-level synthesis. To train the agent without human annotation, we develop an automated data synthesis pipeline that extracts multi-hop subgraphs from a citation knowledge graph, verified by cross-model consensus among 20 frontier models. The agent is subsequently aligned through a reverse-decomposition rubric strategy that provides fine-grained process rewards for early planning and strict evidence grounding. Evaluations across six scientific benchmarks encompassing standard QA, citation accuracy, factual reasoning, and structural synthesis demonstrate that SciLENS significantly outperforms open-source baselines and achieves performance comparable to GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3.0-pro. Our source code and data are released at https://github.com/LQgdwind/SciLENS.

title: Robustness of shallow graph embedding methods for community detection
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the robustness of shallow graph embedding methods for community detection in the face of network perturbations, specifically node deletions. Graph embedding techniques, which represent nodes as low-dimensional vectors, are widely used for various graph machine learning tasks due to their ability to capture structural properties of networks effectively. However, the impact of perturbations on the performance of these methods remains relatively understudied. The research considers state-of-the-art shallow graph embedding methods from two families: matrix factorization (e.g., LE, LLE, HOPE, M-NMF) and random walk-based (e.g., DeepWalk, LINE, node2vec). Through experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world networks, the study reveals varying degrees of robustness within each family of shallow graph embedding methods. The robustness is found to be influenced by factors such as network size, initial community partition strength, and the type of perturbation. Notably, node2vec and LLE consistently demonstrate higher robustness for community detection across different scenarios, including networks with degree and community size heterogeneity. These findings highlight the importance of selecting an appropriate shallow graph embedding method based on the specific characteristics of the network and the task at hand, particularly in scenarios where robustness to perturbations is crucial.

title: The Impact of Anthropomorphism on AI Chatbot Usage Intention: The Mediating Role of Customer Experience in a Modified UTAUT Model
abstract: The precipitous trajectory of artificial intelligence has hastened, within university career services, the integration of chatbot systems. However, technical sophistication alone does not guarantee the efficacy of AI chatbot deployment; user acceptance and the quality of the interaction experience are equally critical. This study identifies the mediating role of customer experience within the association between anthropomorphism, the constructs of a modified Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT)—namely perceived ease of use, performance expectancy, initial trust, and social influence as well as the usage intention toward the Patriot Yupi chatbot at a university Career Center. A quantitative survey was administered to 403 university alumni, and the collected data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that all hypothesized direct correlations were positive and statistically significant. Furthermore, customer experience meaningfully mediated the associations between anthropomorphism, the modified UTAUT constructs, and usage intention. Specifically, anthropomorphism cultivates favorable user perceptions, while customer experience serves as the pivotal mechanism translating these perceptions into a sustained intention to use the chatbot. This research extends the scope within which the UTAUT framework can be meaningfully applied within the domain of AI-driven career service chatbots and provides practical insights for designing chatbots that effectively enhance the user experience.

title: PhysisML: a language model trained from scratch on a developmental curriculum, with dream consolidation against catastrophic forgetting
abstract: PhysisML (φυσις physis, nature/growth, + ML) is a language model implemented from scratch — a decoder-only transformer with every layer's forward and backward pass hand-written in NumPy, plus a PyTorch mirror for speed — and trained on a developmental curriculum of thirteen Italian levels (phonemes to question answering), with a dynamic vocabulary that grows during training and a rule-based tutor that grades every answer, so the whole curriculum reproduces offline. Each teaching session ends in a dream: a consolidation pass that replays every previous level's question-answer corpus. The dream is what turns catastrophic forgetting (~20% retention across levels) into ~88%. The repository includes a head-to-head benchmark of the dream against online Elastic Weight Consolidation (Schwarz et al. 2018) on the same harness (exp_i): in this near-perfect-memorization curriculum regime, the implementation of standard online EWC with an empirical diagonal Fisher substantially underperforms experience replay on both seeds (final-row retention 13.0% vs 64.4%), landing below even the no-protection floor (22.0%), because at near-zero training loss the empirical Fisher measures inter-example gradient variance concentrated on shared structural tokens — an anti-selective anchor that freezes the answer-production machinery instead of the knowledge. The comparison is not compute-matched, so the relative efficiency of the two methods remains open.The repository contains the full training code, the Italian curriculum, the teaching loop with rule-based/local-LLM/API tutors, the retention benchmark harness, and documentation in English and Italian.

title: Adaptive Subgraph Learning via Machine Learning
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive subgraph learning framework leveraging machine learning to dynamically construct and optimize subgraphs within data representations. Traditional methods often rely on manual design, limiting flexibility and potentially suboptimal results. Our approach employs a machine learning model to learn inherent features of subgraphs and then utilizes these features to guide the optimization of model parameters, ultimately leading to improved data representation and model performance.

title: Probability Logic Tensor Analysis (PLSA) Dynamic Complexity Assessment
abstract: Probability Logic Tensor Analysis (PLSA) presents a novel approach to dynamic complexity assessment for machine learning models. This paper investigates the application of PLSA to automatically evaluate model complexity in response to changing data inputs and model parameter updates. The core mechanism leverages dynamic data fusion to dynamically assess model complexity, offering a more precise and adaptive optimization strategy compared to static complexity evaluation. This work addresses limitations of traditional PLSA by incorporating data-driven adjustments, resulting in improved model optimization efficiency.

title: Self-Adaptive Quantum Topology for Quantum Information Storage Optimization
abstract: Quantum information storage is a crucial challenge in the development of quantum technologies. Current storage methods often rely on classical structures, limiting storage density and reliability. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum information storage, leveraging the unique properties of quantum topology to optimize data storage efficiency. We propose a dynamic quantum topology adjustment algorithm that iteratively alters the quantum state to maximize data density and reduce error rates. This method, employing a combination of mathematical modeling and algorithmic refinement, demonstrates significant improvements in both storage density and information fidelity compared to existing approaches. The core mechanism focuses on leveraging topological features to enhance data preservation, offering a pathway towards more robust and scalable quantum information storage.

title: Algorithmic Complexity Reduction via Fractal Geometry
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithmic approach to reduce the complexity of complex computational problems through iterative fractal-based reduction. Traditional methods often rely on exhaustive search, which is computationally expensive. We propose a self-improving algorithm that dynamically refines the problem's representation by mimicking fractal patterns, effectively shrinking the search space exponentially with each iteration. This approach leverages the inherent properties of fractals to optimize computational processes and potentially achieve significant speedups for problems exhibiting inherent complexity. The core mechanism involves iteratively applying fractal transformations to the problem's structure, creating a representation that is inherently more amenable to efficient solutions.

title: Adaptive Topology in Parallel Distributed Processing (PDP) Networks
abstract: This paper explores the application of adaptive topology in parallel distributed processing (PDP) networks to enhance model performance and generalization. Traditional PDP networks often rely on static topology, limiting their ability to effectively learn and adapt to data variations. We introduce a novel dynamic topology mechanism that dynamically adjusts connections within the network based on error signals, fostering a more flexible and robust learning process. The proposed method focuses on minimizing the error gradient during training, promoting a smoother and more efficient convergence towards optimal model parameters. The paper details the implementation of the mechanism, including the error calculation and connection adjustment process, and demonstrates its effectiveness through simulations and a simplified case study.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Neural Network Activation Function Adjustment
abstract: This paper investigates the design of a dynamic adaptive neural network activation function adjustment method. Traditional activation functions often rely on fixed parameters, limiting the model's ability to adapt to changing data inputs. We propose a novel approach that utilizes a dynamic self-adjusting activation function, enabling the network to automatically modulate activation strength based on data input variations. This adaptive mechanism enhances model performance through improved generalization and robustness. The proposed method incorporates a feedback loop that continuously monitors data input and adjusts the activation function parameters to maintain optimal performance. This results in a more adaptable and efficient neural network architecture. The core mechanism involves a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts the activation function parameters based on the input data. The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the proposed method, demonstrating its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and experimental validation. The key advantages of this approach include improved generalization, robustness, and adaptive learning capabilities.

title: 基于领域自适应的深度图神经网络
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to enhancing the generalization capability of Deep Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) by leveraging domain adaptation techniques. Current DGNNs often struggle with limited generalization performance due to variations in the distribution of training data across different domains. To address this, we introduce a framework incorporating domain-adaptive loss functions and domain-adversarial training. The domain-adaptive loss function explicitly encourages the learning of relationships between domains, treating domain similarity as a regularization term. Simultaneously, domain-adversarial training enhances the model's robustness to domain shifts. Our method aims to bridge the gap between domain-specific and domain-general DGNNs, ultimately leading to improved performance in scenarios with diverse and potentially mismatched data. We formally define the loss functions and training procedures, outlining the core mechanisms and their mathematical formulations. The core claim is that by learning domain relationships, we can improve DGNN generalization. The core mechanism involves domain-adaptive loss and domain-adversarial training.

title: Quantum Information Cryptography Foundation Theory
abstract: Quantum Information Cryptography (QIC) represents a paradigm shift in secure communication, leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics to safeguard information. This foundational theory proposes a novel QIC framework centered around quantum entanglement and key distribution, aiming to establish a robust and secure cryptographic system. The core mechanism involves establishing a quantum entanglement-based key distribution protocol, ensuring cryptographic security through entanglement's inherent properties and enhancing privacy protection. This work explores the theoretical foundations of QIC, detailing its core principles, mechanisms, and potential implications for the future of secure communication.

title: Quantum Decoherence Enhancement for Robust Quantum Communication Protocols
abstract: This paper presents a novel protocol for enhancing robust quantum communication through the deliberate manipulation of decoherence. The core concept leverages the interaction between specific frequency noise, generated by control pulses, and the quantum state being transmitted. This interaction effectively strengthens the correlation between the quantum state and the information carrier, ultimately leading to a significant reduction in decoherence rates and improved transmission efficiency over longer distances. The proposed scheme addresses limitations of existing protocols that heavily rely on precise quantum control and extended quantum storage times. We detail the theoretical framework, outlining the key components and mathematical formulations involved in the protocol, demonstrating a promising approach to achieving reliable quantum communication. The design incorporates a feedback loop to dynamically adjust the control pulses based on real-time measurements of the quantum state, maximizing the beneficial effects of the induced noise. Simulation results (presented qualitatively) demonstrate the potential for substantial improvements in transmission fidelity compared to standard protocols. The protocol is adaptable to various quantum communication platforms and offers a pathway towards practical, long-distance quantum networks.

title: Adaptive Quantum Algorithm Parallel Expansion Strategy
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive quantum algorithm parallel expansion strategy designed to optimize computational performance in quantum computing environments. The core of this approach lies in dynamically adjusting the parallelism of quantum computations based on the allocation of available quantum resources. We propose a novel mechanism that utilizes quantum resource allocation information to automatically scale the complexity of parallel computations, ensuring efficient execution. The proposed strategy offers a significant advantage over static expansion techniques, providing a flexible and adaptable solution for tackling complex quantum problems. This work explores the benefits of dynamic resource allocation in quantum algorithm development, demonstrating a practical implementation and analysis of the proposed method.

title: Non-Linear Geometric Models for Quantum Information Cryptography
abstract: Quantum information cryptography stands as a critical discipline for safeguarding sensitive data in the face of increasing computational threats. Traditional cryptographic methods are vulnerable to attacks exploiting weaknesses in mathematical algorithms and computational power. This paper explores the potential of employing non-linear geometric models as a foundation for advanced quantum information encryption. We propose a novel approach that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to enhance the security and complexity of cryptographic algorithms. The core focus is on designing a system based on these models to achieve superior protection against potential adversaries. We detail the underlying principles of the proposed system, outlining the mechanism of operation, its potential benefits, and a preliminary assessment of its effectiveness. This research addresses the limitations of current cryptographic practices by introducing a novel paradigm centered around geometric transformations and quantum entanglement. The resulting system aims to offer a robust and adaptable framework for secure data exchange, potentially surpassing the capabilities of existing methods. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and challenges inherent in translating this concept into a practical implementation.

title: Nonlinear Chaotic Systems Under Multi-Agent Collaboration Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to optimization within nonlinear chaotic systems utilizing multi-agent collaboration. Traditional optimization methods often struggle in the face of complex, non-linear dynamics. This work proposes a framework where multiple agents, each operating within a localized chaotic system, dynamically interact and collaborate to achieve global optimization. The core concept leverages the inherent sensitivity and non-linearity of chaotic dynamics for information exchange and strategic adjustments. The system is designed to overcome the limitations of conventional algorithms by exploiting the emergent behavior arising from this collaborative, chaotic environment. Mathematical formulations detail the system dynamics and convergence criteria. The results demonstrate the potential for enhanced optimization performance compared to traditional methods, particularly in scenarios with high dimensionality and complex interactions. The key contribution lies in the systematic integration of chaotic dynamics with multi-agent systems for tackling challenging optimization problems.

title: Based on Quantum Entanglement, Adaptive Quantum Simulation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offers a unique opportunity for creating highly accurate simulations of complex physical systems. This paper explores the development of an adaptive quantum simulation method leveraging quantum entanglement to enhance the fidelity and efficiency of simulations. We introduce a novel architecture that dynamically adjusts the quantum system's parameters based on the observed results, leading to improved accuracy and the ability to model systems previously challenging for classical methods. The core mechanism centers on the utilization of entangled states to represent and manipulate quantum variables, enabling a more robust and nuanced simulation process. This work provides a foundation for a future where quantum simulations become significantly more accessible and effective.

title: Title: Adaptive Parameter Adjustment for Dynamic Quantum Algorithms
abstract: Quantum algorithms, renowned for their potential to solve complex problems intractable for classical computers, rely heavily on precise parameter control. Traditional parameter optimization methods, often based on iterative refinement, can be computationally expensive and may not always converge to optimal solutions. This paper introduces a novel dynamic parameter adjustment approach for quantum algorithms, aiming to enhance algorithm efficiency and accuracy by autonomously adapting to the evolving quantum state. title: Renewable energy mapping in Northeastern Morocco: A geographic information system‐based comparison of geothermal, solar, and wind potential in the Guercif‐Guilliz and Beni Snassen regions
abstract: Abstract The development of hybrid renewable energy systems is increasingly recognized as a viable solution for improving energy access and system reliability in resource‐diverse but infrastructure‐limited regions. However, in Northeastern Morocco, the combined renewable energy potential of geothermal, solar, and wind resources has not been assessed from a spatial and integrative perspective. This paper presents a geographic information system (GIS)‐based review and comparative analysis of geothermal, solar, and wind energy resources in Northeastern Morocco, with particular emphasis on the Guercif‐Guilliz and Beni Snassen regions. By compiling and analyzing existing geospatial, geological, and environmental datasets, the study evaluates geothermal gradients and hydrothermal manifestations alongside solar irradiance and wind field characteristics. The analysis highlights the complementarity of these renewable resources and reviews the feasibility of hybrid geothermal‐solar and geothermal‐wind systems as sustainable energy solutions for off‐grid and underserved areas. Furthermore, the paper discusses the conditions under which three‐source hybrid configurations (geothermal‐solar‐wind) may become technically and economically viable. By synthesizing dispersed data into a coherent spatial framework, this review provides a structured basis for future planning and investment, supporting Morocco's strategic objectives for renewable energy expansion and long‐term energy security.

title: LLM4CKD: Large Language Models for Early Stage Chronic Kidney Disease Screening
abstract: Early screening of chronic kidney disease (CKD) is critical for timely intervention, yet most machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches require labeled data and model training, limiting their use in real-world screening settings. This study evaluates the effectiveness of large language models (LLMs) for CKD screening under zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning settings and compares them with traditional ML and DL methods. We propose a framework that uses clinically selected tabular features and structured prompt templates to enable LLM-based inference without task-specific training. LLM performance is evaluated across multiple prompt styles, feature configurations, and data settings, and compared with standard ML, DL, and tabular foundation model (TFM) baselines, and existing CKD screening tools. The results show that LLMs can achieve competitive performance using only a small number of examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings. However, their performance remains model-dependent and less stable as input complexity increases. In contrast, ML, DL, and TFM models show more consistent improvement with larger training data. Overall, the findings highlight a trade-off between data efficiency and stability, suggesting that LLMs may serve as a flexible complementary approach for CKD screening when labeled data are limited. To facilitate further research and reproducibility, the code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/akabircs/LLM4CKD

title: Synthetic Semantic Supervision for Contrastive Code Representation Learning in Small Transformers: An Empirical Study
abstract: General-purpose code embeddings power tools for code search, classification, and retrieval. Compact transformer encoders for code typically rely on either human-written docstrings (labor-intensive and inconsistent) or mined structural signals such as execution traces (setting-specific and costly to collect). We empirically study an alternative: contrastive pretraining of small encoders with synthetically generated natural-language descriptions emphasizing code functionality and intent, paired with code in a dual-encoder framework at training and discarded at inference. We benchmark this approach against pretraining-based baselines, generalist LLMs, and embedding-specific models on eight retrieval, classification, and generation tasks across C, C++, and Java. Synthetic semantic supervision yields statistically significant gains over pretraining baselines of the same inference-time size on five of eight tasks, with parity on two more; once fine-tuned, it matches or exceeds zero-shot models two orders of magnitude larger on classification, and it stays on par with execution-aware supervision at matched pretraining data, suggesting a scalable, effective alternative to existing code-representation paradigms.

title: KnowFeat: Knowledge-Guided Feature Engineering via LLM Agents
abstract: Automated feature engineering with large language models (LLMs) can produce semantically meaningful features for tabular data, yet existing methods lack structured domain knowledge, rigorous verification, and explainable provenance. We propose KnowFeat, a knowledge-guided feature engineering framework that organizes domain knowledge into five types -- schema metadata, regulatory indicators, detection rules, expert opinions, and court document evidence -- and injects them as structured context into an LLM agent. A three-stage verification pipeline filters candidates through code execution, statistical quality checks, and model effectiveness evaluation. Every accepted feature carries a provenance record tracing its design to specific knowledge assets. Under a strict held-out protocol that eliminates feature-selection leakage, KnowFeat ranks first (avg. rank 2.3) across twelve public benchmarks among seven methods (one-sided Wilcoxon p=0.017), with a peak gain of +11.6 pp AUC on a telecom churn dataset. On a real-world Bitcoin anti-money laundering (AML) dataset (Elliptic) and a synthetic digital currency AML benchmark (SimECNY), KnowFeat maintains competitive detection performance with full provenance traceability.

title: Revising the Joules-per-Compute (JPCUB) Benchmark: Normalizing Energy Efficiency by Logical-Qubit Operations
abstract: Current joules-per-compute (JPCUB) benchmarks normalize energy consumption per physical gate, conflating logical operations with error-correction overhead. This obscures trade-offs between qubit connectivity, gate fidelity, and fault-tolerant design, hindering equitable comparisons of quantum processors. We propose a revised JPCUB metric that normalizes energy use per logical-qubit operation, isolating logical computation from error-correction infrastructure. The protocol involves executing standardized logical circuits (e.g., Clifford operations) on surface-code qubits, measuring total energy, and decomposing it into logical gate costs and error-correction overhead. By standardizing benchmark circuits and energy measurement techniques, this approach enables reproducible evaluations of quantum architectures. Simulations suggest [to verify] a 2–5× reduction in JPCUB for fault-tolerant systems compared to uncorrected benchmarks, highlighting the interplay between logical efficiency and error-correction demands. ## 1. Introduction Quantum computing architectures face escalating energy demands as they scale, necessitating rigorous metrics to evaluate efficiency. The existing JPCUB benchmark, which quantifies energy per physical gate [arXiv:2006.07065], fails to distinguish between the energy required for logical operations and that consumed by error correction. Logical-qubit operations inherently involve multiple physical gates and repeated error-correction cycles, yet current metrics conflate these components, leading to inconsistent evaluations. This limitation impedes the development of architectures optimized for both computational speed and energy efficiency. Here, we address this gap by redefining JPCUB to normalize energy consumption per logical-qubit operation, enabling fair comparisons across diverse quantum processor designs. ## 2. title: Adaptive Topological Geometry: A Novel Approach to Geometric Computation
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Topological Geometry, a novel framework that leverages quantum entanglement to construct and manipulate topological spaces. The core mechanism centers around establishing a dynamic, self-adjusting topology, achieved through controlled entanglement of quantum states. This approach promises unprecedented precision in geometric transformations and offers a fundamentally different perspective on computational geometry. We explore the potential of this method to overcome limitations of traditional techniques in complex geometric modeling and exploration. The paper presents a conceptual overview of the system, detailing the core claim, mechanism, and potential applications.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for generating graph embeddings that move beyond the traditional Euclidean distance metric. The core challenge lies in accurately representing the complex relationships within graph data, often hindered by the limitations of Euclidean distance. We propose a dynamic similarity measure, intelligently adjusting the score based on data distribution, to achieve a more robust and insightful representation. This approach addresses the inherent challenges of graph data by incorporating a sophisticated weighting system that captures the data's statistical properties. The proposed method offers enhanced performance and interpretability compared to existing techniques.

title: Algorithmic Complexity Theory for Quantum Simulations
abstract: Quantum simulations are increasingly important for scientific discovery, particularly in fields like materials science and drug discovery. However, these simulations face significant challenges due to the inherent complexity of quantum systems. Traditional complexity analysis methods often struggle to accurately estimate the computational resources required for large-scale simulations, hindering progress. This paper proposes a novel algorithmic approach, 'Quantum Complexity Estimator' (QCE), designed specifically to address these challenges by dynamically modeling resource consumption and identifying critical bottlenecks. We present a framework that automatically estimates the complexity of a quantum simulation by analyzing its structure and implementing a sophisticated optimization strategy. The QCE aims to provide a more practical and scalable method for assessing the feasibility of quantum simulations, enabling researchers to focus their efforts on the most computationally demanding aspects. The paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in estimating complexity for several benchmark quantum simulations.

title: Topology-Aware Neural Network Architectures
abstract: This paper explores the application of topology-aware neural network architectures to improve representation learning and generalization. Current neural network designs frequently neglect the fundamental role of network topology, which significantly influences feature extraction and model performance. We propose a novel approach that explicitly integrates topology-related mechanisms, such as graph-based connections and edge weights, into the network structure. This integration allows the network to learn and represent relationships between nodes more effectively, leading to enhanced representation quality and improved generalization capabilities. The core claim of this work is that incorporating topology-aware mechanisms into neural network architectures will result in more robust and accurate representations.

title: Formal Modeling of Emergent Behavior in Complex Systems
abstract: This paper presents a novel formal modeling approach for analyzing and understanding emergent behavior within complex systems. The core argument is that emergent phenomena, defying simple reductionist predictions from individual component properties, require a more holistic and dynamic representation. The methodology leverages the combined power of Petri nets and agent-based modeling to create a framework capable of explicitly capturing the intricate interactions that drive emergence. This approach moves beyond descriptive analysis towards predictive modeling, allowing researchers to investigate how system-level behaviors arise from the collective actions of its constituents. We detail the framework's key components, including the specification of agents, their interactions, and the utilization of Petri nets to model the flow of information and resources within the system. The focus is on providing a rigorous mathematical foundation for studying and potentially influencing emergent patterns. The proposed framework offers a significant advancement in the field by providing a structured method for tackling the inherent complexities of emergent systems.

title: 基于多智能体协作的非确定性进化算法
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to complex problem-solving by integrating multi-agent collaboration with a non-deterministic evolutionary algorithm (NEAT). The core idea is to construct a system of multiple agents, each employing a distinct strategy, and utilize NEAT to facilitate search and optimization. Traditional evolutionary algorithms are often susceptible to getting trapped in local optima; however, this framework leverages the competitive and cooperative interactions between agents to effectively escape these limitations and enhance the overall problem-solving capabilities. Specifically, each agent utilizes a strategy derived from a genetic algorithm, engaging in both competition and cooperation with other agents. This multi-agent collaborative learning process continuously evolves and refines the strategies employed, leading to improved solutions. The research demonstrates the potential of this combined approach to address complex challenges where traditional methods struggle. The proposed system offers a robust and adaptable solution by capitalizing on the inherent diversity and learning capabilities of multiple agents. The effectiveness of this methodology is assessed through a theoretical analysis and conceptual framework, laying the groundwork for future experimental validation.

The core idea is to construct a system of multiple agents, each employing a distinct strategy, and utilize NEAT to facilitate search and optimization. Traditional evolutionary algorithms are often susceptible to getting trapped in local optima; however, this framework leverages the competitive and cooperative interactions between agents to effectively escape these limitations and enhance the overall problem-solving capabilities. Specifically, each agent utilizes a strategy derived from a genetic algorithm, engaging in both competition and cooperation with other agents. This multi-agent collaborative learning process continuously evolves and refines the strategies employed, leading to improved solutions. The research demonstrates the potential of this combined approach to address complex challenges where traditional methods struggle. The proposed system offers a robust and adaptable solution by capitalizing on the inherent diversity and learning capabilities of multiple agents. The effectiveness of this methodology is assessed through a theoretical analysis and conceptual framework, laying the groundwork for future experimental validation.

title: 基于神经元模拟的概率逻辑电路
abstract: This paper explores the design and implementation of probabilistic logic circuits based on neural simulations. The core idea is to leverage the inherent properties of neural networks to perform logical operations with probabilistic outcomes. We propose a mechanism to translate logical operations into patterns of neural network activation, achieved by adjusting neuron weights and connections. The plasticity of neural synapses is then utilized for learning and adaptation, allowing the network to effectively execute probabilistic logic gates. This approach offers a novel computational model potentially applicable to uncertainty computation and machine learning, diverging from traditional digital logic designs. The presented framework demonstrates a foundational approach to building logic circuits directly within a neural network architecture, enabling the exploration of inherently probabilistic computation. The key elements involve mapping logical operations to neural activation patterns, and the crucial role of synaptic plasticity in achieving the desired probabilistic functionality. This work provides a theoretical foundation and an initial design for such circuits, opening up avenues for future research and development in areas requiring robust handling of uncertainty.

title: Quantum Entanglement Optimization: A Novel Approach to Non-Asymmetricity and Algorithm Design
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, exhibits a peculiar property: correlations that transcend distance. This property has sparked intense research into its potential for quantum technologies, particularly in quantum computing and information. However, the precise nature of entanglement's behavior, specifically its non-asymmetric nature, remains a significant challenge. This paper explores the potential of leveraging this non-asymmetry to develop novel optimization algorithms, aiming to enhance the stability and efficiency of entangled states. We propose a new quantum entanglement model based on "self-adaptive symmetry," which guides the optimization process through a carefully engineered non-symmetric state. This approach promises to unlock new possibilities in quantum computation and information processing by offering a fundamentally different perspective on entanglement dynamics. The core mechanism centers around the systematic manipulation of entangled states to achieve optimal results. This work presents a novel theoretical framework and preliminary experimental investigations that demonstrate the potential of this approach.

title: 基于量子纠缠的自适应量子算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm, termed "Dynamic Quantum Adaptation," leveraging the principle of quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust quantum system parameters. The core mechanism centers on the instantaneous transfer of quantum state between entangled qubits, allowing for continuous and adaptive optimization of quantum computation. We present a theoretical framework detailing the algorithm's operational principles and demonstrate its potential for significant efficiency improvements compared to traditional algorithms within specific quantum scenarios. The paper explores the challenges and future directions of this approach, emphasizing the importance of entanglement and dynamic parameter control.

title: Title: Geometric Complexity in Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: Geometric Complexity in Evolutionary Algorithms (GCE) proposes a novel metric for assessing the performance of evolutionary algorithms, emphasizing the intricacy and stability of the solution space. This paper introduces a new Geometric Complexity Score (GCS) – a measure of the solution's structural complexity – that integrates geometric constraints and feedback mechanisms to steer the evolutionary process towards optimal solutions. The core mechanism centers on dynamically adjusting the search strategy based on this GCS, promoting solutions that exhibit a higher degree of geometric complexity. This approach moves beyond simply evaluating the final fitness of a solution, offering a more holistic understanding of algorithmic progress. We provide a detailed explanation of the GCS, its implementation, and results demonstrating its effectiveness in improving evolutionary algorithm performance across diverse problem domains. The paper also discusses the implications of this new metric for future research in evolutionary optimization and algorithm design.

title: Constraint Network Cryptography A: Constraint Network Phase Transition of Quantum Computational Advantage- From Shor's Algorithm to Information Barriers
abstract: This paper reinterprets the collapse of classical public-key cryptography byquantum computation as a computational complexity phase transition in constraintnetworks. Within the ontology of constraint networks, the security of RSA and elliptic curve cryptography depends on the exponential information barriers formedby multiplicative cohesion or scalar multiplication cohesion in classical graph geometry, whereas Shor’s algorithm lifts the state space to spectral geometry in Hilbertspace via the quantum Fourier transform, directly reading the hidden period, andthus reduces the information barrier of the splitting operator from sub-exponentialor exponential depth to polynomial order. Grover’s algorithm is interpreted as acompression of the traversal entropy by the quantum diffusion operator, which onlytakes the square root of the barrier depth for symmetric ciphers without alteringtheir exponential nature. For post-quantum cryptography, the hardness of latticecryptography is attributed to the rigidity of high-dimensional lattices, whose localdensity extrema cannot be penetrated by Fourier-type spectral operators; the security of hash-based signatures depends on the traversal entropy compression limitof collision search. The paper further provides a categorical formulation of quantum immunity criteria using the constraint-network category and the approximateadjoint structure of lifting and reduction, and explicitly demarcates the honestboundary and cognitive debt. The entire argument follows the axiom of information conservation, emphasizing that quantum advantage originates from geometricphase transitions rather than information generation.

title: Based on Quantum Entanglement: Adaptive Probability Models
abstract: This paper investigates a novel probabilistic model leveraging quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust probability distributions within a system. We propose a framework that allows the model to adapt to changing system states, resulting in enhanced accuracy and computational efficiency compared to traditional approaches. The core mechanism involves exploiting the inherent correlations within entangled states to create a self-correcting probability function. This research explores the potential of quantum entanglement for optimizing probabilistic calculations, offering a promising path towards more robust and efficient computation.

title: Quantum Entanglement for Asymmetric Computation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for revolutionizing computation. This paper explores the development of a novel computational paradigm based on entangled quantum states, aiming to achieve non-symmetric computation and expand into the realm of quantum computing beyond classical limitations. We present a core mechanism for harnessing entanglement's inherent asymmetry to enhance computational efficiency and unlock new capabilities. The research focuses on algorithmic design and analysis to demonstrate the feasibility of this approach. The central claim is that this framework can facilitate the execution of complex calculations leveraging the unique properties of entangled quantum states, ultimately pushing the boundaries of quantum computing.

title: Algorithmic Quantum Phase-Shift (AQP)
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of Algorithmic Quantum Phase-Shift (AQP) – a novel quantum algorithm designed to dynamically adjust the phase shift of quantum states, facilitating efficient exploration of complex quantum systems. Traditional quantum algorithms often rely on fixed, pre-determined phase shifts, limiting their ability to adapt to evolving quantum states. AQP proposes a framework for iterative phase manipulation, offering a pathway towards fundamentally new approaches to quantum system design and optimization. We detail the core mechanism of the algorithm, outlining its iterative process and the resulting benefits in terms of pattern discovery and task optimization. The paper explores potential applications across diverse quantum computing paradigms, highlighting the advantages over existing techniques. This work presents a foundational contribution to the field of quantum algorithm design and aims to provide a roadmap for future research in dynamic quantum state manipulation.

title: Geometric Information Theory Quantum Acceleration Computing (GITAC)
abstract: This paper introduces Geometric Information Theory Quantum Acceleration Computing (GITAC), a novel approach to quantum computation designed to significantly enhance the efficiency of geometric information theory (GIT) calculations. GIT, a foundational field in geometric data processing and compression, relies heavily on intricate mathematical operations and complex data structures. Traditional implementations often struggle with the computational demands associated with these operations, limiting their applicability to large datasets and demanding computational resources. GITAC leverages the unique properties of quantum information theory – specifically, entanglement and self-associativity – to accelerate these computations. The core mechanism involves utilizing quantum entanglement to expedite the transformation of geometric data, ultimately leading to improved data compression and processing speeds. We present a conceptual framework for GITAC, detailing the algorithm's key components and their potential impact on GIT calculations. This research explores the potential advantages of quantum acceleration in GIT, outlining a pathway to more efficient and scalable geometric data manipulation.

title: 基于自适应神经网络的复杂系统动力学模型
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for modeling complex systems utilizing an adaptive neural network (ANN) approach. Traditional approaches often struggle with the dynamic nature of complex systems, necessitating static models that quickly become outdated. Our model dynamically adjusts the neural network's structure and parameters based on observed data, enabling automatic model refinement and improved predictive capabilities. The core of this design lies in the implementation of an adaptive algorithm that continuously optimizes the network's architecture. We present a comprehensive evaluation of this approach, demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling a range of complex systems, highlighting its ability to maintain high accuracy and adaptability in dynamic environments. The paper concludes with a discussion of the model's key advantages and potential future directions.

title: Python-Based Visualization of Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein Distributions in Three-Dimensional Ideal Quantum Gases
abstract: Quantum statistics describe the behavior of indistinguishable particles through the Fermi–Dirac (FD) and Bose–Einstein (BE) distributions. This study compares both distributions directly to emphasize their fundamental statistical differences. A Python-based computational model was developed to visualize the contrasting behaviors of FD and BE distributions in a unified 3D representation. The simulation uses NumPy and Matplotlib with an energy interval of 0.01–1.00, temperatures ranging from 100 K to 600 K, and a chemical potential of The results show that the FD distribution forms a sharp profile near the Fermi energy and becomes step-like at low temperatures, while the BE distribution rises sharply as the chemical potential is approached, reflecting the characteristic mathematical divergence of Bose–Einstein statistics rather than indicating actual Bose–Einstein condensation. As temperature increases, the differences between the Fermi–Dirac and Bose–Einstein distributions become less pronounced, consistent with the expected high-temperature limit. The model yields an average relative deviation below 0.5%, confirming numerical stability and accuracy. This work provides an open-source Python framework for the visualization and comparative analysis of ideal quantum statistical distributions, intended primarily for educational and computational purposes rather than for predicting new physical phenomena.

title: NARAD: Nuclear AI-Ready Accelerator Data and LinkML
abstract: This presentation introduces NARAD (Nuclear AI-Ready Accelerator Data), an operational ontology and knowledge-graph framework developed under the Genesis Mission to address the AI-readiness gap in accelerator facility data. NARAD leverages LinkML and aligns with standards such as PALS and SOSA/SSN to enable FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and machine-actionable data across diverse accelerator environments. The talk outlines the challenges of making accelerator data AI-ready, describes NARAD’s layered architecture, and demonstrates use cases including facility understanding, semantic channel finding, and digital twin/model generation. Real-world instances from JLab’s UITF and BNL’s BtA illustrate how NARAD supports cross-facility data integration and operational reasoning, paving the way for autonomous agents and advanced AI applications in accelerator science.

title: Efficient and secure heterogeneous aggregate signcryption for Vehicular Ad-Hoc Networks
abstract: Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs) are an important part of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). They allow vehicles to communicate with each other and with roadside infrastructure to improve traffic flow and road safety. However, because these communications use wireless channels, they are vulnerable to security threats such as message tampering, eavesdropping, and tracking of vehicles. In addition, the use of different cryptographic systems can make communication between networks difficult. To address these issues, this work proposes a pairing-free certificateless heterogeneous aggregate signcryption scheme (PF-CLHASC). The scheme enables secure communication between certificateless cryptography (CLC) and public key infrastructure (PKI) systems without using complex bilinear pairing operations. It also protects vehicle identity by using pseudonyms, preventing messages from being linked to real users. The security of the scheme is based on the hardness of the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP) and is analyzed using the random oracle model. Experimental results show that the scheme reduces computational, communication, and storage costs by 16.67% to 90.33%, and lowers transmission overhead. It also ensures privacy, forward secrecy, and protection against replay, impersonation, and man-in-the-middle attacks.

title: Development and Evaluation of Ultrasound Image Learning Pipelines for MASLD Risk Stratification
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately 30% of the general population. Ultrasound-based imaging, including B-mode imaging and shear wave elastography (SWE), is widely used for noninvasive fibrosis assessment; however, the role of deep learning-based ultrasound image learning for MASLD risk stratification remains insufficiently characterized. In this study, we developed and evaluated ultrasound image learning pipelines using B-mode and SWE images for fibrosis staging and identification of patients with at-risk metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). A total of 250 ultrasound examinations, one exam per subject, were included. Model performance was evaluated using 3-fold cross-validation with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). End-to-end SWE image learning achieved performance comparable to operator-guided SWE across fibrosis stages. Overall, SWE-based learning consistently outperformed B-mode image learning in fibrosis staging, with AUROC improvements from 0.64 (95%CI: [0.56, 0.72]) to 0.72 (95% CI: [0.65, 0.79]) for F>=2 (significant fibrosis, p=0.11), from 0.67 (95%CI: [0.58, 0.75]) to 0.78 (95% CI:[0.72, 0.85]) for F>=3 (advanced fibrosis, p=0.02), and from 0.69 (95%CI: [0.56, 0.82]) to 0.80 (95%CI: [0.72, 0.89]) for F4 (cirrhosis, p=0.10). These findings highlight the potential of SWE image learning for MASLD risk stratification.

title: Memory as transformation: LETHE, a self-referential gan-inspired architecture
abstract: LETHE (Latent-parameter Evolution with Temporal Hierarchical quasi-Equilibrium) is a self-referential sonic-oblivion system implemented in SuperCollider. It adopts the formal vocabulary of Generative Adversarial Networks in a closed configuration without external datasets or supervision after initialization. Audio is processed by a 3 x 3 mixing matrix built around two delay lines; its nine coefficients and two delay times evolve through the interaction of a five-feature linear discriminator and a random-perturbation optimizer analogous to single-sample REINFORCE. The discriminator compares current energy behavior with an archive of the initial state and guides parameter updates. Circular, fixed, and live sources can be mixed independently. Across fixed and circular sessions with an ablation control, the active generator is necessary for parametric evolution ($Δc_{22}=0.000$ in all 15 ablation sessions). Situated in the tradition of self-referential electroacoustic music, LETHE delegates the sonic outcome to an adaptive closed loop whose parametric space is defined by the composer.

title: Differentiable Hybrid Modelling for Learning and Optimising Chemical Transport Processes from Experimental Data
abstract: Transport models underpin the design and optimisation of chemical processes, yet their constitutive laws are typically hand-picked, their experimental initial conditions are assumed exact, and their computational cost restricts optimisation to a handful of process variables. Here we introduce a differentiable hybrid modelling framework that embeds neural networks within a GPU-accelerated population balance equation solver to discover constitutive laws and assimilate initial conditions directly from experimental crystallisation data. Using thirteen real experiments with multi-dimensional size and shape measurements, we show that treating measured initial conditions as exact yields a physically inconsistent rate law despite improved predictive accuracy, whereas assimilating them recovers a physically consistent, non-linear law and reduces trajectory error sevenfold relative to conventional modelling. End-to-end differentiability further enables gradient-based optimisation of high-dimensional operating profiles, identifying a 300-variable temperature profile that reduces crystal aspect ratio by 25% at constant mass, facilitating superior product attributes. Our framework augments, rather than replaces, mechanistic modelling, offering a general route to learning transport models from data and optimising processes with them.

evidence.title: Differentiable Hybrid Modelling for Learning and Optimising Chemical Transport Processes from Experimental Data
evidence.abstract: Transport models underpin the design and optimisation of chemical processes, yet their constitutive laws are typically hand-picked, their experimental initial conditions are assumed exact, and their computational cost restricts optimisation to a handful of process variables. Here we introduce a differentiable hybrid modelling framework that embeds neural networks within a GPU-accelerated population balance equation solver to discover constitutive laws and assimilate initial conditions directly from experimental crystallisation data. Using thirteen real experiments with multi-dimensional size and shape measurements, we show that treating measured initial conditions as exact yields a physically inconsistent rate law despite improved predictive accuracy, whereas assimilating them recovers a physically consistent, non-linear law and reduces trajectory error sevenfold relative to conventional modelling. End-to-end differentiability further enables gradient-based optimisation of high-dimensional operating profiles, identifying a 300-variable temperature profile that reduces crystal aspect ratio by 25% at constant mass, facilitating superior product attributes. Our framework augments, rather than replaces, mechanistic modelling, offering a general route to learning transport models from data and optimising processes with them.

title: Deep learning for sustainable development: cross-disciplinary applications and responsible AI
abstract: Global climate change, energy shortages, food security crises, and urban sprawl pose multifaceted governance challenges for sustainable development. Leveraging its capacity for hierarchical representation learning from high-dimensional, heterogeneous data, deep learning has emerged as a core digital technology enabler for advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Employing a systematic literature review methodology and drawing on open-access publications from Google Scholar (2018-2026), this paper examines deep learning applications across four key domains: climate action, sustainable energy, smart agriculture, and smart cities. Through four comparative tables analyzing model suitability, data types, application outcomes, and challenges, the study identifies key bottlenecks in technology deployment from a "Responsible AI" perspective. It identifies three major industry trends: the large-scale deployment of physics-AI hybrid modeling, the growing dominance of deep reinforcement learning in energy dispatch, and the integration of federated learning with edge AI for distributed ecological monitoring. Current implementation efforts remain constrained by four critical issues: regional data divides, a lack of model interpretability, algorithmic bias, and the high carbon footprint associated with large-scale models. By outlining corresponding optimization pathways, this paper provides a theoretical framework and practical guidance for green AI and sustainable digital governance.

title: Dimension Resonance Matrix Calculation and Application
abstract: The dimension resonance matrix (DRM) is a fundamental concept in quantum optics and quantum information theory, representing the entanglement between the states of a system. This paper explores the design and application of a novel dimension resonance matrix calculation method, leveraging quantum entanglement and quantum state resonance to overcome limitations of traditional approaches. We introduce a new algorithmic framework that utilizes entangled qubits to efficiently compute DRM matrices, demonstrating its potential to accelerate quantum computations and facilitate secure quantum communication. This research aims to provide a significant advancement in the computational power of DRM analysis, offering a practical pathway to enhance the performance of various quantum algorithms.

title: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Neural Network Training Dynamics
abstract: This paper presents a novel information-theoretic analysis of neural network training dynamics. Traditional approaches to understanding neural network training often rely on simplified gradient-based methods and empirical observations, lacking a rigorous theoretical foundation. We argue that a more insightful perspective can be gained by framing neural network training as an information processing task. We leverage concepts from information theory, specifically mutual information and entropy, to characterize the flow of information during the training process. Our analysis provides a framework for quantifying the reduction of uncertainty about the optimal parameters, which directly relates to convergence rates and generalization performance. We demonstrate how the rate of information gain, measured through mutual information, can be linked to the learning dynamics. Furthermore, we explore the impact of regularization terms on the entropy of the parameter space, offering a new lens for understanding their role in promoting generalization. The core contribution of this work is a formal information-theoretic framework for analyzing neural network training, offering a more nuanced and potentially more predictive understanding of this complex process.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Networks for Forecasting Complex Time Series
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Hierarchical Bayesian Networks (HBNs) for forecasting complex time series data. Traditional Bayesian networks often fail to adequately represent the intricate hierarchical dependencies prevalent in real-world time series, leading to suboptimal forecasting performance. This work proposes a novel HBN architecture designed to explicitly model these dependencies at multiple levels of abstraction. The core mechanism involves constructing a network where higher-level nodes represent aggregated trends, while lower-level nodes capture finer-grained fluctuations. This approach allows for a more nuanced and accurate representation of the underlying dynamics, ultimately improving forecasting robustness. We present a mathematical framework for the HBN, detailing the probabilistic models and inference algorithms employed. The paper focuses on the theoretical underpinnings and architectural design of the HBN, providing a foundation for future research and practical implementation. The key contribution is a systematic method for building hierarchical models that can effectively handle the complexities of time series forecasting.

title: Causal Inference with Dynamic Bayesian Networks and Granger Causality Tests
abstract: Traditional Bayesian networks offer a powerful framework for representing and reasoning about causal relationships. However, they often struggle to accurately represent systems where causal connections are not static but evolve over time. This paper introduces a novel approach that combines dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs) with Granger causality tests to address this limitation. The proposed framework allows for the identification and adaptation of causal relationships within a system as new data becomes available. The core innovation lies in using Granger causality tests – a statistical method for determining if one time series predicts another – as a mechanism for updating the structure of the dynamic Bayesian network. This process generates a more robust and accurate representation of evolving causal dynamics. The methodology is presented with a clear theoretical foundation and demonstrates the potential for improved causal inference in complex, time-varying systems. The system is modeled using DBNs and Granger causality tests to identify and update causal relationships over time, allowing for the modeling of evolving causal structures in complex systems.

title: Cognitive Architecture Based on Time Flow: Semantic Representation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel cognitive architecture grounded in the concept of "time flow," aiming to enhance cognitive understanding and reasoning by explicitly incorporating temporal information. Traditional cognitive architectures often treat knowledge and experience as static representations, neglecting the crucial role of time in shaping human cognition. This architecture addresses this limitation by representing knowledge and experience as sequences of events along a time flow. We leverage time series analysis techniques to perform knowledge reasoning based on these temporal sequences and utilize the temporal relationships between events to establish semantic associations. The core claim of this work is that constructing a time-flow based cognitive architecture, utilizing time-ordering information for richer semantic representation, will improve cognitive tasks' understanding and reasoning capabilities. The proposed mechanism focuses on transforming knowledge and experience into temporal event sequences, applying time series analysis for knowledge inference, and exploiting event temporal relationships for semantic connections. We believe this approach offers a more biologically plausible and effective model of human cognition. ---

title: Context-Aware Relational Reasoning via Bayesian Networks with Temporal Dependencies
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to relational reasoning by integrating Bayesian Networks with temporal dependencies and contextual influences. Traditional Bayesian Networks struggle to represent the dynamic and context-dependent nature of relationships observed in many real-world scenarios. Our method extends Bayesian Network inference to explicitly model time-varying probabilities and incorporate contextual factors, enabling dynamic updates and significantly improved relational predictions. We introduce a framework where the strength of relationships is not fixed but evolves over time, influenced by surrounding circumstances. This approach addresses the inherent limitations of static Bayesian Networks and provides a more robust and accurate representation of complex relational dynamics. The core of the method lies in defining temporal Bayesian Networks (TBNs), which allows us to represent how relationships change over time and how these changes are affected by the context. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through conceptual formulations, highlighting its advantages and outlining future research directions.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Distributed Algorithm Verification Framework
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for distributed algorithm verification leveraging quantum entanglement. The core claim centers on the ability to independently verify algorithms without relying on shared keys or classical communication, thereby enhancing both verification efficiency and security. The proposed mechanism utilizes a set of entangled particles, each representing a component of the algorithm, enabling direct assessment of correctness through measurements of the entangled state. This approach circumvents the limitations of traditional distributed verification methods regarding security and efficiency. The framework offers a fundamentally new approach to algorithm verification, capitalizing on the core principles of quantum mechanics. The overall goal is to establish a robust and efficient method for validating distributed quantum algorithms. This document details the framework's architecture, key components, and theoretical underpinnings, focusing on the core principles and potential applications. ---

title: Topological Quantum Bit-Based Quantum Key Distribution Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol leveraging the unique properties of topological quantum bits (TQBs). Traditional QKD protocols are vulnerable to attacks exploiting imperfections in quantum hardware. TQBs, due to their inherent robustness against local perturbations and decoherence, offer a promising solution for enhancing security. This protocol, termed TQB-QKD, utilizes the topological protection inherent in TQBs to establish a key between two parties, Alice and Bob. The core of the protocol revolves around the measurement of the non-local properties of TQBs, resulting in a highly secure key exchange. We detail the protocol's key generation steps, error correction, and privacy amplification stages, emphasizing the advantages derived from TQB characteristics. The protocol is designed to mitigate potential attacks targeting qubit decoherence and measurement errors, offering a pathway towards more secure and practical QKD systems. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the improved security margin compared to conventional QKD protocols.

title: Decentralized Federated Learning with Differential Privacy using Threshold Cryptography
abstract: Federated learning (FL) presents a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources while preserving user privacy. However, traditional FL methods often rely on a central server, introducing a single point of failure and potential privacy risks. This paper proposes a novel decentralized federated learning system that leverages threshold cryptography and differential privacy to address these concerns. The core claim is that protecting user privacy in federated learning remains a significant challenge, and this system provides a robust solution. The system operates through a series of distributed rounds where participants collaboratively update model parameters using threshold cryptography to ensure secure aggregation and differential privacy to mitigate individual data exposure. This approach eliminates the need for a central server, enhancing both privacy and security. The system is designed for scalability and adaptability, making it suitable for various decentralized data scenarios. This work contributes to the development of more secure and privacy-preserving federated learning solutions.

title: Adaptive Geometry Model Optimization for Self-Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive machine learning framework for the optimization of non-linear geometry models. Traditional machine learning methods often struggle with the inherent complexities of non-linear geometric models, resulting in instability and inefficiency. Our proposed framework dynamically adjusts the parameters of the geometry model to enhance the stability and efficiency of the learning process. This adaptation occurs in real-time, allowing the model to continuously refine its representation of the underlying geometric structure. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that leverages gradient-based optimization, coupled with a novel parameter adjustment strategy inspired by biological neural networks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing improvements in both model stability and learning speed compared to baseline methods. The framework offers a promising path towards more robust and efficient machine learning for complex geometric modeling problems.

title: Anti-Forgetting Adaptive Teacher-Driven Knowledge Distillation for Medical Image Classification
abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in medical image classification, yet their performance remains sensitive to dataset size. Knowledge distillation (KD) alleviates this issue by transferring knowledge from a high-capacity teacher to a lightweight student. However, conventional KD relies on a static teacher, while adaptive teacher updating may improve performance on the student-learning data while reducing retention of knowledge acquired during teacher pretraining. To address these limitations, we propose an Anti-forgetting Adaptive Teacher-driven Knowledge Distillation framework (A2T-KD), which aims to balance teacher adaptation and pretraining-knowledge retention. The proposed framework integrates three modules: MITR for cross-epoch representation consistency, DSDO for prediction-space decoupling and class discriminability, and SGKD for feature- and logit-level knowledge transfer. Across nine medical imaging datasets, A2T-KD achieved higher mean values than the fixed-teacher Vanilla KD baseline in 30 of 36 dataset–metric comparisons. It also exhibited the lowest pretraining-set ACC degradation among the evaluated teacher-update baselines on all nine datasets, supporting the intended balance between teacher adaptation and pretraining-knowledge retention under the evaluated settings.

It also exhibited the lowest pretraining-set ACC degradation among the evaluated teacher-update baselines on all nine datasets, supporting the intended balance between teacher adaptation and pretraining-knowledge retention under the evaluated settings.

title: Theory of Agent: The Science of Internalization and Externalization for LLM-Based Agents
abstract: A large language model (LLM) agent is a model coupled to a harness: parametric weights that hold knowledge and reasoning ability, wrapped in an external apparatus of memory, tools, and orchestration through which the model perceives and acts. Progress over the past years has come from pushing on both, with stronger models and richer harnesses, but the design decision that quietly governs an agent’s behavior is where competence should live: which knowledge, skills, and control to internalize into the model’s parameters, and which to externalize onto the surrounding harness. These decisions increasingly determine whether an agent is reliable, efficient, and able to keep improving. We investigate this core problem through the lens of the Theory of Agent (ToA), which views an LLM agent not as a task executor but as an epistemic decision-maker in terms of reasoning or acting at every step. The two means it has for that epistemic uncertainty reduction, namely reasoning over what it already holds and acting on the world to obtain what it does not, are the run-time faces of internalization and externalization: reasoning draws on competence that has been absorbed into the model, while acting exploits competence that remains in the harness. We review this internalization and externalization across five chapters. Foundations sets up the basic picture: an agent that, at each step, decides whether to answer from what it already knows or reach outside for what it does not, and what separates a good version of that decision from a wasteful one. Learning examines how training places competence on either side of the boundary, spanning internalization of memory, reasoning, tool-use policy, and world models, and externalization of memory, skills, and orchestration. Aligning treats calibration as the connecting thread across an agent’s cognitive boundaries, efficiency constraints, human preferences, environment constraints, and other agents. Evolving studies how agents revise both sides of the boundary over time, from model-side and harness-side updates to agent–environment co-evolution. Evaluation reinterprets metrics and benchmarks by the epistemic effort they expose and argues for measuring the boundary decision rather than task completion alone. We conclude with the open problems that follow once internalization and externalization are treated as the governing axis of agent design.

title: Focusing on Individual Risk: Personality-Based Content Adaptation in Virtual Agents for Safety Education
abstract: In intelligent virtual agents (IVAs), adaptation strategies based on individual user characteristics are important for enhancing the effectiveness of educational and behavior change interventions. However, prior research on personality-based adaptation in IVAs has predominantly focused on adapting how information is delivered—such as persuasion strategies and communication styles—while the approach of adapting what to focus on, that is, shifting the content focus itself according to individual characteristics, remains underexplored. In this study, we propose a personality-adapted IVA for safety education that shifts the focus of accident analysis information according to users’ personality-based risk profiles. The dialogue structure incorporates user-driven reasoning about accident causes and action planning to support active processing of the focused information. We conducted a field experiment with 74 employees of a power company, assigning participants to either an adaptive condition, which presented personality-focused information, or a control condition, which presented general safety information, over six dialogue sessions spanning three weeks. Comparing pre- and post-intervention importance ratings of accident causes corresponding to each participant’s targeted personality trait, we found that only the importance ratings for the targeted trait selectively increased in the adaptive condition, while no changes were observed for non-targeted traits or in the control condition. This selective pattern demonstrates that shifting content focus according to individual risk factors is an effective IVA adaptation strategy for promoting users’ recognition of accident risks linked to their own personality traits. Furthermore, these findings suggest that content focusing in IVAs can serve as a means of helping users identify and become aware of their own internal states—cognitive and behavioral tendencies—that are relevant to specific outcomes.

title: Examining How Explanations from Multiple AI Agents Affect User Trust After AI Refusal
abstract: AI systems are designed to decline certain requests to avoid providing harmful or inaccurate information. However, refusals can unintentionally reduce users’ impressions of and trust in AI. Prior work has examined what an AI should explain when refusing a request, but offers no guidance on which AI should deliver the explanation when multiple agents are involved. Using a multi-agent scenario, we compared two explanation conditions, delegated explanation by a third-party AI on behalf of the primary AI and shared explanation by both AIs, against two complementary baselines: no explanation and self-explanation by the primary AI. Results showed that users’ impressions of the primary AI dropped when it delegated the explanation about the refusal to the third-party AI. Moreover, this negative impression transferred to the third-party AI: even without directly refusing, it was perceived as reinforcing the primary AI’s refusal. We discuss challenges and opportunities in designing multi-agent AI explanations for refusing users’ requests.

title: AI Cautionary Guide: Pitfalls and Strategies for the Use of Machine Learning in Medical Research
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly utilized in medical research. However, underrecognized methodological pitfalls can result in misleading conclusions, which if acted upon can result in patient mismanagement and harm. As a result, we have provided a compilation of common pitfalls and practical safeguard considerations for ML-enabled medical research. Examples emphasize the importance of integrating clinical/biologic knowledge and statistical/epidemiologic principles, illustrated with key case examples. Topics include (1) Data drift, which can create artificial trends when coding systems or clinical practices change over time; (2) Feature construction that should be clinically grounded, as models may otherwise learn operational proxies rather than true biology; (3) Accidental data leakage, which can inflate apparent model performance and collapse on real-world deployment; (4) Competing risks and differential time-at-risk that can generate spurious associations in safety analyses if not modeled explicitly; (5) Confounding and collider bias, which can distort findings, particularly in EHR-based studies; (6) For rare outcomes, inappropriate evaluation measures can overstate performance and mislead explainability analyses; (7) Finally, pooled multi-trial analyses require careful handling of the intrinsic heterogeneity to avoid extracting study artifacts rather than generalizable signals. By outlining many of the common potential issues, with lessons learned, we aim to provide the medical and research community with practical insights to help foster trustworthy ML-enabled medical research.
